analysis.one_liner: Bans selling tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, to anyone under 21, with FDA enforcement.
analysis.headline: The Tobacco to 21 Act, backed by 97 Democrats and Republicans, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on its introduction day and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal to sell any tobacco product — cigarettes, cigars, smokeless tobacco, or e-cigarettes — to anyone under 21, and requires photo ID for anyone under 30. It directs the FDA to enforce the ban through undercover compliance checks, retailer inspections, and penalties for stores that violate it, and it lets states keep stricter laws of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Teenagers and young adults, who are most likely to get hooked on nicotine; their families; and the public health system, since the bill's findings cite projections that a national Tobacco 21 law would produce about 223,000 fewer premature deaths and 45,000 fewer lung cancer deaths among people born between 2000 and 2019, plus near-term drops in preterm birth, low birth weight, and sudden infant death syndrome.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens and young adults at risk of nicotine addiction

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits sale of all tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, to anyone under 21, closing the gap that let 18-to-20-year-olds buy for themselves and their younger peers.
Requires photo-ID age verification for purchasers under 30 and puts the FDA in charge of enforcement, with undercover checks, retailer inspections, and penalties for repeat violations.

The bill's findings cite the National Academy of Medicine's estimate that a national age-21 law would cut smoking prevalence by about 12% over time and prevent roughly 223,000 premature deaths among people born 2000-2019.
Cites the 78% surge in youth e-cigarette use from 2017 to 2018, with more than 3.6 million teenagers vaping, as part of the problem the ban targets.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers and e-cigarette companies lose sales to the roughly 18-to-20-year-old market; retailers — including small convenience stores and gas stations — bear compliance costs and federal fines for selling to minors, including under undercover checks; and adult smokers under 21 lose the legal ability to buy. Taxpayer money funds the added FDA enforcement work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies, vape makers, and retailers

drawbacks.text: The ban restricts a legal product for adults aged 18 to 20, which opponents view as government telling legal adults they cannot choose for themselves.

Retailers bear the enforcement burden: ID checks for everyone who looks under 30, plus FDA undercover buys and fines, fall on store clerks and owners — often small convenience and gas station businesses.
It addresses only the point of sale; it does not by itself restrict e-cigarette flavors, marketing, or product design, which the bill's own findings identify as central to youth vaping.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and well-documented in the bill's own findings: 94% of adult smokers start before 21, nicotine addiction takes hold most easily in adolescence, and a national age-21 law is projected to save hundreds of thousands of lives. The costs are real but narrower — lost sales for a product that kills roughly 480,000 Americans a year, and compliance burdens on retailers. On balance the benefits clearly outweigh the costs, with the main fair criticism being that a sales-age ban alone does not address flavors and marketing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee the week it was introduced, and it sat there until the 116th Congress ended without a hearing-driven vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on April 30, 2019, joined by six original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Chris Stewart, Jaime Herrera Beutler, Bill Flores, and Rob Wittman.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Health the next day.
It gathered 97 cosponsors — 76 of 231 House Democrats and 21 of 197 House Republicans — but the action history shows no further movement after the subcommittee referral.

The bill's findings note that three-quarters of American adults, including 7 in 10 smokers, favor raising the tobacco sale age to 21, and that twelve states and more than 110 localities had already done it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, e-cigarette companies, and retailers who sell to 18-to-20-year-olds were better off, since the sale ban never advanced and their customer base stayed open during the two-plus years the bill sat in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and vape sellers who kept those sales

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 76 of 231 House Democrats and 21 of 197 House Republicans signed on — and no member publicly opposed the bill on the record; it stalled in committee without a vote, so the opposition that mattered was never roll-call opposition.

industries.note: Cigarette, cigar, and smokeless tobacco companies would lose sales to the 18-20 age group, which the bill's findings describe as the critical window when experimenters become daily smokers. The bill's findings also note the industry's history of challenging tobacco control measures in court and marketing to young people, so its interest runs against the bill's goal of keeping nicotine away from teens.
Vaping products fall under the bill's tobacco-product definition, and with youth vaping up 78% in a year, these companies would lose the bulk of their underage-and-young-adult customer pipeline.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers, including convenience stores and gas stations
industries.note: Retailers would lose sales to 18-20-year-old customers and absorb compliance costs — ID checks for anyone who looks under 30 — while facing FDA undercover checks and fines, including escalating penalties for repeat violations. Their burden is the enforcement mechanism the public benefit depends on, so their position is real but also the price of the policy working.
